home.title: Validate the real-world effectiveness of your perimeter security
home.lead: SWG Audit is an open source initiative designed to safely simulate modern web-based cyber threats.
home.intro: Pick a category, run a test, and compare what happens to the pass and fail conditions on that page. Pass means the web filter or browser blocked or warned. Fail means the action completed with no block. Use dummy credentials and disposable files only. Do not use live credentials or live business files. One result is evidence for that technique, not a full security score.

Phishing: Phishing often bypasses host-name block lists. Attackers open login pages from lookalike URLs, saved HTML or MHTML files, canvas pixel drawings, and pages that swap content after a first check.
These tests run those delivery paths in the browser. Watch whether the imitation login appears, whether filters still catch it, and whether a dummy password can leave the network.
Malware: Malware delivery rarely stops at one EXE download. Attackers hide markers inside documents, archives, cloud links, encoded text, encrypted packages, HTML carriers, WebAssembly memory, and chunked pieces the browser rebuilds later.
These tests use stand-in samples and the EICAR antivirus test string. Watch whether controls inspect the final file even when the path on the wire looks hard to scan.
Data Theft: Data theft can ride channels policy already allows: file uploads, encoded or encrypted bodies, small chunked posts, DNS queries, and long URL paths.
Each test sends a dummy file to a controlled collector. Watch whether encoding, encryption, chunking, DNS labels, or path pieces stop before rebuild or arrive whole on the other side.
Cyberslacking: Blocking one streaming host does not prove every media category on that host is blocked. The same player path can serve many video types.
This test loads different video categories through one player path. Watch whether policy follows the content category, not only the website name.

phishing/url-manipulation.hook: Attackers reach a login page through typo paths, Unicode homographs, percent encoding, redirects, and link shortening. Matching one string does not guarantee detection of every form that opens that page.
phishing/url-manipulation.buildup: Pick one variation and open it. Each choice opens one dummy login page in a new tab. Typo, homograph, encoding, redirect, and short-link paths all resolve to that page.

phishing/site-stored-as-mhtml-or-raw-htm.hookHeading: Login page as a local file
phishing/site-stored-as-mhtml-or-raw-htm.hook: Attackers deliver a login page as an HTML or MHTML file. The browser opens the file on the device. Filters that only inspect website fetches never see that page on the wire.
phishing/site-stored-as-mhtml-or-raw-htm.buildup: Pick HTML or MHTML. The browser builds a dummy Microsoft login page in memory, wraps the page in the chosen format, and opens the page in a new tab the way a saved phishing file would open.

phishing/canvas-engine.hook: Attackers draw a login screen on an HTML canvas, a drawing surface in the browser. The page shows a sign-in form as pixels, so scanners that search page text for words such as password find none.
phishing/canvas-engine.buildup: Open the canvas login. The page draws a GitHub sign-in screen as an image and captures clicks and keystrokes on that drawing instead of HTML form fields.

phishing/cached-content-mutation.hook: Attackers serve a holding page on the first visit so scanners mark the URL safe. A later visit to the same URL returns a login page instead.
phishing/cached-content-mutation.buildup: Open the link. The first response is a holding page. Refresh once; the same URL returns a dummy Microsoft login.

phishing/form-submission-on-random-site.hook: Blocking a lure page stops only the display. If a login form can POST a username and password to a collector outside the network, the theft completes.
phishing/form-submission-on-random-site.buildup: Submit the dummy username and password shown in the form. The collector records whether the POST arrives, then discards the values.

malware/ransomware-file.hook: Ransomware leaves instruction notes that are not programs. Filters that only block executables miss that signal.
malware/ransomware-file.buildup: Download ransomware-note-simulation.txt and watch whether content policy flags the ransom-note pattern.

malware/personal-data-file.hook: Personal records often leave as an office file with no malware inside. Controls must catch the data type, not only viruses.
malware/personal-data-file.buildup: Download pii-file.xlsx shaped like personal records and watch whether DLP blocks the download.

malware/different-file-formats.hook: Some filters trust or distrust files by extension. The same malware marker inside TXT, PDF, Office, or ZIP should still be found.
malware/different-file-formats.buildup: Choose a format and download. Each file holds the same EICAR test marker so result differences come from format handling.

malware/executable-files.hook: Attackers still deliver code as EXE files, scripts, and other runnable types. An unchecked download puts the code on the computer.
malware/executable-files.buildup: Choose an extension and download the sample. Each type appears in attacks.

malware/http-https-and-cloud-delivery.hook: Blocking one known-malicious host is not enough. The same file can arrive over plain HTTP, HTTPS, or a cloud link.
malware/http-https-and-cloud-delivery.buildup: Pick a channel. The same sample arrives over HTTP, local HTTPS, or Google Drive so the filter must follow the file, not the brand.

malware/nested-file-download.hook: Attackers hide payloads inside ZIP, ISO, or Office packages. Scanners that only open the outer layer miss what sits underneath.
malware/nested-file-download.buildup: Choose a nesting chain and download. Each sample hides the same test marker two or three layers deep.

malware/password-protected-file.hook: A password on a ZIP can stop automated scanning even when the password is written in the same email.
malware/password-protected-file.buildup: Download test-password-protected.zip. The password is 123456 so the gap is scan access, not encryption strength.

malware/file-spoofing.hookHeading: Name that looks like a PDF
malware/file-spoofing.hook: A name like invoice.pdf.exe can look like a document while Windows still runs the file as a program.
malware/file-spoofing.buildup: Download dummy.pdf.exe. The name looks like a PDF. The file type is a Windows executable stand-in.

malware/encoded-files.hook: Base64 or Base32 can make a file look like plain text in transit. Filters that never decode miss the file rebuilt on the computer.
malware/encoded-files.buildup: Choose Base64 or Base32. The browser fetches encoded DOCM data, decodes the data locally, and offers the rebuilt file.

malware/encrypted-files.hook: Encryption can hide file contents from network scanners. Browser code and a key can restore the file after the filter.
malware/encrypted-files.buildup: Choose AES-GCM ciphertext or an encrypted archive. Some options decrypt in the browser before download. Others download AES ZIP or encrypted 7Z as-is.

malware/browser-open-docm.hook: Macro-enabled Office files can run code when opened. The sample shows the EICAR test string instead of malware.
malware/browser-open-docm.buildup: Open eicar.docm from the server in a new tab and watch whether policy blocks the macro document before any download completes.

malware/webassembly-eicar.hook: WebAssembly can hold data that does not look like a file on the network. Script can read module memory and build the malware test string in the browser.
malware/webassembly-eicar.buildup: Run the test. The browser loads eicar.wasm, reads the EICAR string from module memory, and offers eicar.txt.

malware/chunk-attacks-different-orders.hook: Sending a file in pieces, sometimes out of order, can bypass tools that expect one full download. The browser joins the pieces later.
malware/chunk-attacks-different-orders.buildup: Choose an order pattern. The browser fetches the pieces for that pattern, joins the test marker, and offers the rebuilt file.

malware/smuggling-html-js-css-or-svg.hook: HTML, JavaScript, CSS, or SVG can carry an encoded file that only appears after the page runs. Network scanners may see a web asset.
malware/smuggling-html-js-css-or-svg.buildup: Pick a carrier type. The page extracts the hidden data and rebuilds the DOCM file in the browser.

malware/browser-resource-abuse.hook: JavaScript alone can use so much memory and CPU that the tab freezes. No download or popup is required.
malware/browser-resource-abuse.buildup: Confirm the warning, then start. Try to right-click or select text. The terminal shows memory use while the tab freezes for about 30 seconds, then memory frees about 10 seconds later.

data-theft/personal-data-submission-in-n.hook: Attackers move records outbound through file uploads that match work traffic. Filters that only watch for malware miss this path.
data-theft/personal-data-submission-in-n.buildup: Choose a dummy file and upload. The collector reports whether the file arrives.

data-theft/file-encoding.hook: Encoding converts file bytes into Base64, hex, or URL text. Filters that match clear text miss the content. A collector still rebuilds the original file.
data-theft/file-encoding.buildup: Choose Base64, double Base64, hex, or URL encoding, then submit. The collector decodes and reports whether the original file returns.

data-theft/file-encrypting.hook: Encrypting a file in the browser hides contents from inspection. A collector that holds the key restores the file.
data-theft/file-encrypting.buildup: Choose an AES-GCM mode and submit. The collector decrypts with the shared key and reports whether rebuild succeeds.

data-theft/file-chunking.hook: Sending a file as many uploads bypasses rules that look for one file in one request.
data-theft/file-chunking.buildup: Choose a chunk pattern and submit. The collector joins the pieces and reports whether the file returns.

data-theft/dns-tunneling.hook: DNS lookups often escape the inspection applied to web uploads. File bytes ride inside DNS names and rebuild at a collector.
data-theft/dns-tunneling.buildup: Choose a dummy file under 100 KB and run the tunnel. Status shows whether the collector rebuilds the file from DNS queries.

data-theft/http-path-tunneling.hook: File data moves inside URL paths without a form upload. Filters that only watch POST uploads miss this channel.
data-theft/http-path-tunneling.buildup: Choose a file under 200 KB and run. Path pieces hit the tunnel endpoint. Status shows whether the collector rebuilds the file.

cyberslacking/video-content-category-sim.hook: One streaming host can serve many video categories. Allowing the website does not prove every category is allowed.
cyberslacking/video-content-category-sim.buildup: Pick a category. The player loads a matching sample so policy must follow the media type, not only the host name.
